notes.front: What is a cloud computing activity, in the international reference architecture?
notes.back: A specified pursuit or set of tasks, which must have a purpose and deliver one or more outcomes.
notes.explanation: Activities are carried out using functional components, and the standard describes them role by role.
notes.example: Like the tasks on a job description: 'monitor service' is one task, and a job is a bundle of them.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3502 | ISO/IEC 17789:2014, Cloud computing reference architecture, clause 7.2.1, Cloud computing activities, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the application capabilities type?
notes.back: A cloud capabilities type in which the cloud service customer can use the cloud service provider's applications.
notes.explanation: Capability types classify what a cloud service offers the customer according to the resources used.
notes.example: Like hiring a car with a driver: you use the journey, the driver handles the rest.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clauses 3.2.1 and 3.2.4, PDF p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the platform capabilities type?
notes.back: A capabilities type in which the customer can deploy, manage and run its own or acquired applications, using languages and execution environments the provider supports.
notes.explanation: The customer brings the application; the provider supplies the programming languages and runtime it runs on.
notes.example: Like renting a fitted kitchen: you cook your own recipes with the appliances provided.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 3.2.31, PDF p. 10
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the infrastructure capabilities type?
notes.back: A capabilities type in which the cloud service customer can provision and use processing, storage or networking resources.
notes.explanation: It offers the most basic resources; what runs on them is up to the customer.
notes.example: Like renting an empty warehouse with power and water: what you put inside is your business.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 3.2.25, PDF p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Software as a Service (SaaS)?
notes.back: The consumer uses the provider's applications running on a cloud infrastructure.
notes.explanation: The applications can be reached from various client devices, through a thin client such as a web browser or through a program interface.
notes.example: An online accounting package a small business logs into through its browser.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Service Models, PDF p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Software as a Service (SaaS). The capability provided to the consumer is to use the provider’s applications running on a cloud infrastructure 2. The applications are accessible from various client devices through either a thin client interface, such as a web browser (e.g., web-based email), or a program interface.

notes.front: What is Platform as a Service (PaaS)?
notes.back: The consumer deploys its own or acquired applications onto the cloud infrastructure, using languages, libraries, services and tools the provider supports.
notes.explanation: The consumer controls the deployed applications, and possibly settings of the hosting environment, but not the infrastructure beneath.
notes.example: A developer pushes a web application's code to a hosted runtime, which runs it without her touching any servers.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Service Models, PDF p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: languages, libraries, services, and tools supported by the provider.3 The consumer does not manage or control the underlying cloud infrastructure including network, servers, operating systems, or storage, but has control over the deployed applications and possibly configuration settings for the application-hosting environment.

notes.front: What is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?
notes.back: The consumer provisions processing, storage, networks and other fundamental computing resources, on which it can deploy and run arbitrary software.
notes.explanation: That software can include operating systems as well as applications.
notes.example: A company rents virtual servers and installs its own operating system and database on them.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Service Models, PDF p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS). The capability provided to the consumer is to provision processing, storage, networks, and other fundamental computing resources where the consumer is able to deploy and run arbitrary software, which can include operating systems and applications.

notes.front: What is a public cloud?
notes.back: A deployment model in which cloud services are potentially available to any cloud service customer and resources are controlled by the cloud service provider.
notes.explanation: Public clouds have very broad boundaries: customer access has few, if any, restrictions.
notes.example: Like a public swimming pool: anyone can buy a ticket, and the council runs the pool.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.5, Cloud deployment models, PDF p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a private cloud?
notes.back: A deployment model in which cloud services are used only by a single cloud service customer, which controls the resources.
notes.explanation: Private clouds set a narrowly controlled boundary by limiting the customers to one organisation.
notes.example: Like a pool in a private house: only the household swims, and it decides the rules.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.5, Cloud deployment models, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a community cloud?
notes.back: A deployment model whose services exclusively support, and are shared by, a specific group of customers with shared requirements and a relationship with one another.
notes.explanation: Its resources are controlled by at least one member of that group.
notes.example: Like a swimming club's pool, used only by members of a few clubs that run it together.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.5, Cloud deployment models, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a hybrid cloud?
notes.back: A deployment model that uses at least two different cloud deployment models.
notes.explanation: The deployments stay separate entities but are bound together by technology that enables interoperability and data and application portability.
notes.example: Like a household that swims at home most days and books the public pool for parties.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.5, Cloud deployment models, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is interoperability, as a cross-cutting aspect of cloud computing?
notes.back: The ability of a cloud service customer to interact with a cloud service and exchange information in a prescribed way, with predictable results.
notes.explanation: The standard's terms section (clause 3.1.5) also borrows a wider definition from another international recommendation: two or more systems exchanging information and mutually using what was exchanged.
notes.example: Like a plug that fits the socket and delivers the voltage the kettle expects.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Cloud computing cross cutting aspects, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is portability, as a cross-cutting aspect of cloud computing?
notes.back: The ability of customers to move their data or applications between cloud service providers at low cost and with minimal disruption.
notes.explanation: How much cost and disruption is acceptable may vary with the type of cloud service being used.
notes.example: Like moving house when all your furniture is flat-pack and fits the new rooms.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Cloud computing cross cutting aspects, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is reversibility?
notes.back: A process in which customers retrieve their data and application artefacts, and the provider then deletes their data after an agreed period.
notes.explanation: The provider also deletes any cloud service derived data the contract specifies, such as logs of who used the service.
notes.example: Like leaving a rented flat: you take your belongings, and after an agreed time the landlord clears anything left.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clauses 3.2.35 and 3.2.13, PDF pp. 10 and 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is auditability, as a cross-cutting aspect of cloud computing?
notes.back: The capability of collecting and making available the evidence about a cloud service's operation and use that an audit needs.
notes.explanation: Like every cross-cutting aspect, it has to be coordinated across roles and implemented consistently.
notes.example: Like a shop that keeps every till receipt so its accounts can be checked.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Cloud computing cross cutting aspects, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is governance, as a cross-cutting aspect of cloud computing?
notes.back: The system by which the provision and use of cloud services are directed and controlled.
notes.explanation: The standard calls it cross-cutting because of the need for transparency and for aligning governance with service agreements and contracts between customer and provider.
notes.example: Like a board that sets the rules for how a company buys and uses outside services.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Cloud computing cross cutting aspects, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is maintenance and versioning, as a cross-cutting aspect?
notes.back: Maintenance is changing a service or its resources to fix faults or upgrade; versioning labels the service so customers know which version they use.
notes.explanation: The standard gives two reasons for maintenance: fixing faults, and upgrading or extending capabilities for business reasons.
notes.example: Like a phone app's release notes naming version 4.2 and the bugs it fixed.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Cloud computing cross cutting aspects, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is resiliency, as a cross-cutting aspect?
notes.back: The ability of a system to provide and maintain an acceptable level of service when faults affect its normal operation.
notes.explanation: The faults may be unintentional, intentional or naturally caused.
notes.example: Like a hospital that keeps treating patients on generator power during a blackout.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Cloud computing cross cutting aspects, PDF p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a service level agreement (SLA)?
notes.back: A documented agreement between a service provider and a customer that identifies services and service targets.
notes.explanation: It can sit inside a contract or another documented agreement.
notes.example: A promise that a service will be up 99.9% of each month, with credits if it is not.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 3.1.7, PDF p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a multi-cloud deployment, as Special Publication 800-207 describes it?
notes.back: An enterprise with its own local network that uses two or more cloud service providers to host applications, services and data.
notes.explanation: Sometimes the application sits with one provider and its data source with another.
notes.example: A retailer runs its website with one provider and its warehouse database with another.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture (2020), §4.2, Multi-cloud/Cloud-to-Cloud Enterprise, PDF p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: In this use case, the enterprise has a local network but uses two or more cloud service providers to host applications/services and data. Sometimes, the application/service is hosted on a cloud service that is separate from the data source.

notes.front: Into which three groups can all cloud computing activities be categorised?
notes.back: Activities that use services, activities that provide services and activities that support services.
notes.explanation: A party can play more than one role at a time, and may take on only some sub-roles of a role.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3502 | ISO/IEC 17789:2014, Cloud computing reference architecture, clause 8.1, Introduction to roles, sub-roles and cloud computing activities, PDF p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the international reference architecture, how does a sub-role relate to a role?
notes.back: A sub-role is a subset of the cloud computing activities of a given role.
notes.explanation: A role is a set of activities serving a common purpose, and different sub-roles can share a role's activities.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3502 | ISO/IEC 17789:2014, Cloud computing reference architecture, clause 7.2.2, Roles and sub-roles, PDF p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which customer sub-role is the focal point for technical communications between the cloud service customer and the provider?
notes.back: The cloud service administrator.
notes.explanation: Its aim is the smooth running of the customer's cloud services with its existing systems; its activities include monitoring service and administering tenancies.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3502 | ISO/IEC 17789:2014, Cloud computing reference architecture, clause 8.2.1.2, CSC:cloud service administrator, PDF p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which customer sub-role deals mainly with the financial and legal side of using cloud services?
notes.back: The cloud service business manager.
notes.explanation: It aims to meet the customer's business goals cost-efficiently; its activities include selecting and purchasing services and requesting audit reports.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3502 | ISO/IEC 17789:2014, Cloud computing reference architecture, clause 8.2.1.3, CSC:cloud service business manager, PDF p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which customer sub-role integrates cloud services with the customer's existing systems, including application functions and data?
notes.back: The cloud service integrator.
notes.explanation: It is the fourth customer sub-role, alongside cloud service user, administrator and business manager.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3502 | ISO/IEC 17789:2014, Cloud computing reference architecture, clause 8.2.1.4, CSC:cloud service integrator, PDF p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which provider sub-role relies on one or more peer providers to supply part or all of the services it offers?
notes.back: The inter-cloud provider.
notes.explanation: Its main activities are intermediation, aggregation, arbitrage, peering or federation of peer providers' services.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3502 | ISO/IEC 17789:2014, Cloud computing reference architecture, clause 8.3.1.6, CSP:inter-cloud provider, PDF p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which provider sub-role makes sure the customer's and provider's information security policies are aligned and meet the SLA's security requirements?
notes.back: The cloud service security and risk manager.
notes.explanation: It is responsible for managing the risks of developing, delivering, using and supporting cloud services.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3502 | ISO/IEC 17789:2014, Cloud computing reference architecture, clause 8.3.1.7, CSP:cloud service security and risk manager, PDF p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why does the vocabulary standard say the three cloud capabilities types are different from each other?
notes.back: They follow the principle of separation of concerns: they have minimal functionality overlap.
notes.explanation: The standard defines only these three types and warns against confusing them with other ways of grouping cloud services.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.4, Cloud capabilities types and cloud service categories, PDF p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a cloud service category, and how does it relate to the capabilities types?
notes.back: A group of cloud services with some common set of qualities; it can include capabilities from one or more capabilities types.
notes.explanation: The standard names seven representative categories and expects more to appear.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.4, Cloud capabilities types and cloud service categories, PDF p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which cloud service category provides real-time interaction and collaboration?
notes.back: Communications as a Service (CaaS).
notes.explanation: The standard notes that it can provide both the platform and the application capabilities types.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 3.2.18, PDF p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which cloud service category provides the processing resources needed to deploy and run software?
notes.back: Compute as a Service (CompaaS).
notes.explanation: The standard notes that running some software may need capabilities other than processing resources.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 3.2.20, PDF p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which cloud service category provides data storage and related capabilities?
notes.back: Data Storage as a Service (DSaaS).
notes.explanation: It can provide any of the three capabilities types.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 3.2.22, PDF p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which cloud service category provides transport connectivity and related network capabilities?
notes.back: Network as a Service (NaaS).
notes.explanation: Like storage, it can provide any of the three capabilities types.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 3.2.28, PDF p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Software as a Service, what may the consumer possibly still control?
notes.back: Limited user-specific application configuration settings.
notes.explanation: The consumer does not manage the infrastructure, the operating systems or even individual application capabilities.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Service Models, PDF p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: The consumer does not manage or control the underlying cloud infrastructure including network, servers, operating systems, storage, or even individual application capabilities, with the possible exception of limited userspecific application configuration settings.

notes.front: In Special Publication 500-292, who assumes most of the responsibility for managing and controlling a SaaS application and its infrastructure?
notes.back: The SaaS provider.
notes.explanation: Consumers have limited administrative control of the applications.
notes.source: NIST SP 500-292, NIST Cloud Computing Reference Architecture (2011), §2.3, Cloud Provider, PDF p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: The provider of SaaS assumes most of the responsibilities in managing and controlling the applications and the infrastructure, while the cloud consumers have limited administrative control of the applications.

notes.front: In Platform as a Service, what access does the consumer usually have to the infrastructure beneath the platform?
notes.back: No or limited access to it, such as the network, servers, operating systems or storage.
notes.explanation: The consumer controls its applications and possibly some settings of the hosting environment.
notes.source: NIST SP 500-292, NIST Cloud Computing Reference Architecture (2011), §2.3, Cloud Provider, PDF p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: The PaaS Cloud Consumer has control over the applications and possibly some the hosting environment settings, but has no or limited access to the infrastructure underlying the platform such as network, servers, operating systems (OS), or storage.

notes.front: In Infrastructure as a Service, what does the consumer control?
notes.back: Operating systems, storage and deployed applications, and possibly limited control of select networking components such as host firewalls.
notes.explanation: The consumer does not manage or control the underlying cloud infrastructure.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Service Models, PDF p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: The consumer does not manage or control the underlying cloud infrastructure but has control over operating systems, storage, and deployed applications; and possibly limited control of select networking components (e.g., host firewalls).

notes.front: In Infrastructure as a Service, what does the provider control, according to Special Publication 500-292?
notes.back: The physical hardware and the cloud software that makes provisioning possible, such as host operating systems and hypervisors.
notes.explanation: The reference architecture's examples are physical servers, network equipment, storage devices, host operating systems and hypervisors for virtualisation.
notes.source: NIST SP 500-292, NIST Cloud Computing Reference Architecture (2011), §2.3, Cloud Provider, PDF p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: has control over the physical hardware and cloud software that makes the provisioning of these infrastructure services possible, for example, the physical servers, network equipments, storage devices, host OS and hypervisors for virtualization.

notes.front: In the scope-of-control model of Special Publication 500-292, who does the middleware layer stay hidden from?
notes.back: Software as a Service consumers.
notes.explanation: Middleware is used by PaaS consumers and installed, managed and maintained by IaaS consumers or PaaS providers.
notes.source: NIST SP 500-292, NIST Cloud Computing Reference Architecture (2011), §2.7, Scope of Control between Provider and Consumer, PDF p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: The middleware is used by PaaS consumers, installed/managed/maintained by IaaS consumers or PaaS providers, and hidden from SaaS consumers.

notes.front: In the scope-of-control model of Special Publication 500-292, who is the operating system layer hidden from?
notes.back: Both SaaS and PaaS consumers.
notes.explanation: In an IaaS cloud, by contrast, consumers can run one or more guest operating systems virtualised on a single physical host.
notes.source: NIST SP 500-292, NIST Cloud Computing Reference Architecture (2011), §2.7, Scope of Control between Provider and Consumer, PDF p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: The OS layer includes operating system and drivers, and is hidden from SaaS consumers and PaaS consumers. An IaaS cloud allows one or multiple guest OS‟s to run virtualized on a single physical host.

notes.front: Under Special Publication 800-145, whom is a private cloud provisioned for, and where may it sit?
notes.back: Exclusive use by a single organisation with multiple consumers, such as business units; it may be on or off premises.
notes.explanation: It may be owned, managed and operated by the organisation, a third party, or some combination of them.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Deployment Models, PDF p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Private cloud. The cloud infrastructure is provisioned for exclusive use by a single organization comprising multiple consumers (e.g., business units). It may be owned, managed, and operated by the organization, a third party, or some combination of them, and it may exist on or off premises.

notes.front: Under Special Publication 800-145, what do the organisations sharing a community cloud have in common?
notes.back: Shared concerns, for example mission, security requirements, policy and compliance considerations.
notes.explanation: The infrastructure is provisioned for exclusive use by that specific community of consumers.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Deployment Models, PDF p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Community cloud. The cloud infrastructure is provisioned for exclusive use by a specific community of consumers from organizations that have shared concerns (e.g., mission, security requirements, policy, and compliance considerations).

notes.front: Under Special Publication 800-145, where does a public cloud exist?
notes.back: On the premises of the cloud provider.
notes.explanation: It is provisioned for open use by the general public and may be owned by a business, academic or government organisation, or a mix.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Deployment Models, PDF p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Public cloud. The cloud infrastructure is provisioned for open use by the general public. It may be owned, managed, and operated by a business, academic, or government organization, or some combination of them. It exists on the premises of the cloud provider.

notes.front: Under Special Publication 800-145, what example does the definition give of the technology binding a hybrid cloud together?
notes.back: Cloud bursting for load balancing between clouds.
notes.explanation: The binding technology, standardised or proprietary, enables data and application portability between infrastructures that remain unique entities.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Deployment Models, PDF p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Hybrid cloud. The cloud infrastructure is a composition of two or more distinct cloud infrastructures (private, community, or public) that remain unique entities, but are bound together by standardized or proprietary technology that enables data and application portability (e.g., cloud bursting for load balancing between clouds).

notes.front: Can the customer of a private cloud let other parties use it, according to the vocabulary standard?
notes.back: Yes: it may authorise access for other parties, for its own benefit.
notes.explanation: A private cloud may also be owned and operated by the organisation itself or by a third party, on or off premises.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.5, Cloud deployment models, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the multi-cloud case of Special Publication 800-207, how should an application at one provider reach its data source at another?
notes.back: Directly, rather than tunnelling back through the enterprise network.
notes.explanation: The guide gives performance and ease of management as the reasons.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture (2020), §4.2, Multi-cloud/Cloud-to-Cloud Enterprise, PDF p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: For performance and ease of management, the application hosted in Cloud Provider A should be able to connect directly to the data source hosted in Cloud Provider B rather than force the application to tunnel back through the enterprise network.

notes.front: What makes an aspect of cloud computing 'cross-cutting', in the vocabulary standard?
notes.back: It is a behaviour or capability that must be coordinated across roles and implemented consistently.
notes.explanation: Such aspects affect several roles, activities and components at once, so they cannot be assigned to any one of them.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Cloud computing cross cutting aspects, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which cross-cutting aspects does the vocabulary standard single out as major concerns, sometimes impeding cloud adoption?
notes.back: Security, protection of personal data, and governance.
notes.explanation: Many other cross-cutting aspects, combined with the key characteristics, are good reasons for using cloud computing.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Cloud computing cross cutting aspects, PDF p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the availability aspect, who is the 'authorised entity' that must be able to access and use the service on demand?
notes.back: Typically the cloud service customer.
notes.explanation: Availability is the property of being accessible and usable upon demand by an authorised entity.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Cloud computing cross cutting aspects, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the vocabulary standard describe performance as a cross-cutting aspect?
notes.back: A set of behaviours relating to the operation of a cloud service, with metrics defined in an SLA.
notes.explanation: It is one of the standard's key cross-cutting aspects, shared across roles rather than owned by one.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Cloud computing cross cutting aspects, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What range does security cover as a cross-cutting aspect of cloud computing?
notes.back: From physical security to application security.
notes.explanation: The standard lists requirements such as authentication, authorisation, availability, confidentiality, integrity, audit and incident response, among others.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Cloud computing cross cutting aspects, PDF p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between internal and external cloud governance?
notes.back: Internal: design-time and run-time policies so solutions meet expectations. External: an agreement between customer and provider on use of the services.
notes.explanation: Both come from the vocabulary standard's description of governance as a cross-cutting aspect.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Cloud computing cross cutting aspects, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Under the vocabulary standard's definition of data portability, would printing data out and re-keying it count as easy transfer?
notes.back: No. The essence is ease of moving data, ideally in a format the target accepts or can simply convert.
notes.explanation: Data portability is transferring data between systems without having to re-enter it.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 3.2.21, PDF p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is cloud application portability?
notes.back: The ability to migrate an application from one cloud service to another.
notes.explanation: Cloud data portability is the matching term for moving data between cloud services.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clauses 3.2.2 and 3.2.6, PDF p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In what terms does a cloud SLA characterise the quality of the cloud services delivered?
notes.back: A set of measurable properties specific to cloud computing, business and technical, and a given set of roles.
notes.explanation: The roles are the customer and the provider, with their related sub-roles.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Service levels and service level agreement, PDF p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to Special Publication 800-144, who is ultimately accountable for the security and privacy of a service outsourced to a public cloud?
notes.back: The organisation that chose the public cloud.
notes.explanation: Reducing cost may drive the move, but handing over responsibility for security should not; monitoring and addressing security issues stays with the organisation.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-144, Guidelines on Security and Privacy in Public Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Background, PDF p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Reducing cost and increasing efficiency are primary motivations for moving towards a public cloud, but relinquishing responsibility for security should not be. Ultimately, the organization is accountable for the choice of public cloud and the security and privacy of the outsourced service.

notes.front: According to Special Publication 800-144, do existing guidelines for outsourcing still apply when moving to a public cloud?
notes.back: Yes, generally. What changes is the added complexity and difficulty of keeping oversight, accountability and control.
notes.explanation: The steps organisations take remain basically the same as for more traditional outsourced services.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-144, Guidelines on Security and Privacy in Public Cloud Computing (2011), §5, Public Cloud Outsourcing, PDF p. 47
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: The steps that organizations take remain basically the same for public clouds as with other, more traditional, information technology services, and existing guidelines for outsourcing generally apply as well. What does change with public cloud computing, however, is the potential for increased complexity and difficulty in providing adequate oversight

notes.front: How does Special Publication 800-190 describe application containers?
notes.back: A form of operating system virtualisation combined with application software packaging.
notes.explanation: Containers give a portable, reusable and automatable way to package and run applications.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, Application Container Security Guide (2017), Abstract, PDF p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Application container technologies, also known as containers, are a form of operating system virtualization combined with application software packaging. Containers provide a portable, reusable, and automatable way to package and run applications.

notes.front: A customer employee selects and buys a new cloud service and later asks the provider for an audit report. Which customer sub-role is she playing?
notes.back: A: cloud service business manager.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud service business manager
B) Cloud service administrator
C) Cloud service integrator
notes.choicesExplained: B runs the service day to day, for example monitoring it and administering tenancies. C connects cloud services to existing systems.
notes.explanation: Selecting and purchasing services and requesting audit reports are both activities of the business manager.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3502 | ISO/IEC 17789:2014, Cloud computing reference architecture, clause 8.2.1.3, CSC:cloud service business manager, PDF p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A customer uploads its own code to a provider's hosted runtime, which runs it in a language the provider supports. Which capabilities type is this?
notes.back: The platform capabilities type.
notes.explanation: The customer deploys and runs its own application using an execution environment the provider supports.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.4, Cloud capabilities types and cloud service categories, PDF p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Staff log in to a provider's online payroll application and use it as it is. Which capabilities type is this?
notes.back: The application capabilities type.
notes.explanation: The customer uses the provider's application rather than deploying its own or provisioning raw resources.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.4, Cloud capabilities types and cloud service categories, PDF p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A customer provisions virtual disks and network links and decides itself what runs on them. Which capabilities type is this?
notes.back: The infrastructure capabilities type.
notes.explanation: Provisioning and using processing, storage or networking resources is what defines that type.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.4, Cloud capabilities types and cloud service categories, PDF p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team says Data Storage as a Service is 'just infrastructure'. Which capabilities types can it offer, according to the vocabulary standard?
notes.back: Any of the three: infrastructure, platform and application.
notes.explanation: A category can include capabilities from one or more types, so a category name does not fix a single type.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, Annex A, Table A.1, PDF p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A company runs its database on rented virtual servers under Infrastructure as a Service. Who must patch the servers' operating systems?
notes.back: A: the consumer.
notes.choices:
A) The consumer
B) The provider
C) The cloud carrier
notes.choicesExplained: B controls the physical hardware, host operating systems and hypervisors, not the consumer's guest systems. C only provides connectivity and transport of cloud services.
notes.explanation: In IaaS the consumer has control over operating systems, storage and deployed applications.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Service Models, PDF p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: The consumer does not manage or control the underlying cloud infrastructure but has control over operating systems, storage, and deployed applications; and possibly limited control of select networking components (e.g., host firewalls).

notes.front: Users of a hosted email service want a feature changed in the application itself. Under Software as a Service, what can the customer usually change on its own?
notes.back: A: only limited user-specific configuration settings.
notes.choices:
A) Only limited user-specific configuration settings
B) The application's features
C) The servers the application runs on
notes.choicesExplained: B: individual application capabilities are the provider's to control. C: the infrastructure is also the provider's.
notes.explanation: In SaaS the consumer does not control the infrastructure or even individual application capabilities, apart from limited user settings.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Service Models, PDF p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: The consumer does not manage or control the underlying cloud infrastructure including network, servers, operating systems, storage, or even individual application capabilities, with the possible exception of limited userspecific application configuration settings.

notes.front: A start-up wants to run its own web application without managing servers or operating systems, but keep control of the code. Which service model fits?
notes.back: A: Platform as a Service.
notes.choices:
A) Platform as a Service
B) Infrastructure as a Service
C) Software as a Service
notes.choicesExplained: B would leave the operating systems to the start-up. C gives it the provider's application, not its own code.
notes.explanation: PaaS gives control of the deployed applications while the provider manages the network, servers, operating systems and storage.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Service Models, PDF p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: The consumer does not manage or control the underlying cloud infrastructure including network, servers, operating systems, or storage, but has control over the deployed applications and possibly configuration settings for the application-hosting environment.

notes.front: Five regional hospitals with the same privacy and compliance rules set up a cloud used only by them and run by one of them. Which deployment model is this?
notes.back: A: community cloud.
notes.choices:
A) Community cloud
B) Private cloud
C) Public cloud
notes.choicesExplained: B serves a single customer, not five. C is potentially open to any customer, with resources controlled by the provider.
notes.explanation: A community cloud serves a specific group of customers with shared requirements, and at least one member controls the resources.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.5, Cloud deployment models, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A bank builds a cloud in a third party's data centre that only its own business units use, and the bank controls the resources. Which deployment model is this?
notes.back: A: private cloud.
notes.choices:
A) Private cloud
B) Public cloud
C) Community cloud
notes.choicesExplained: B: location off premises does not make it public; public means open to any customer with provider-controlled resources. C serves a group of several customers.
notes.explanation: It serves a single customer, which controls the resources; a private cloud may be run by a third party and sit off premises.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.5, Cloud deployment models, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Anyone with a credit card can sign up for a provider's storage service, and the provider controls all the resources. Which deployment model is this?
notes.back: A: public cloud.
notes.choices:
A) Public cloud
B) Hybrid cloud
C) Community cloud
notes.choicesExplained: B combines at least two deployment models. C limits participation to a group with shared concerns.
notes.explanation: Services potentially available to any customer, with resources under the provider's control, define a public cloud.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.5, Cloud deployment models, PDF p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A retailer runs its shop on its private cloud and overflows to a public cloud at peak times, with technology linking the two. Which deployment model is this?
notes.back: A: hybrid cloud.
notes.choices:
A) Hybrid cloud
B) Multi-cloud
C) Community cloud
notes.choicesExplained: B means using two or more providers; here the point is a private and a public cloud bound together. C serves a group of organisations with shared concerns.
notes.explanation: A hybrid cloud uses at least two deployment models that stay separate but are bound together by technology.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Deployment Models, PDF p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Hybrid cloud. The cloud infrastructure is a composition of two or more distinct cloud infrastructures (private, community, or public) that remain unique entities, but are bound together by standardized or proprietary technology that enables data and application portability (e.g., cloud bursting for load balancing between clouds).

notes.front: A firm keeps its office network, hosts its customer application with one provider and the application's database with another. What deployment is this?
notes.back: A: multi-cloud.
notes.choices:
A) Multi-cloud
B) Community cloud
C) Private cloud
notes.choicesExplained: B is a single cloud shared by a group of customers. C is used by one customer that controls the resources; neither involves two providers.
notes.explanation: The enterprise uses two or more cloud service providers to host its applications and data.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture (2020), §4.2, Multi-cloud/Cloud-to-Cloud Enterprise, PDF p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: In this use case, the enterprise has a local network but uses two or more cloud service providers to host applications/services and data.

notes.front: A customer ends its contract, downloads all its data and application artefacts, and after 90 days the provider deletes everything it held. Which cross-cutting aspect is this?
notes.back: A: reversibility.
notes.choices:
A) Reversibility
B) Interoperability
C) Resiliency
notes.choicesExplained: B is about exchanging information with a service and getting predictable results. C is about keeping service running despite faults.
notes.explanation: Retrieving data and artefacts, followed by deletion after an agreed period, is the reversibility process.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Cloud computing cross cutting aspects, PDF p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Before signing, a customer checks that the provider will collect and hand over logs and records an auditor would need. Which cross-cutting aspect is it checking?
notes.back: A: auditability.
notes.choices:
A) Auditability
B) Governance
C) Portability
notes.choicesExplained: B is the system for directing and controlling cloud use. C is about moving data or applications between providers.
notes.explanation: Auditability is the capability of collecting and making available the evidence needed to audit a service's operation and use.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Cloud computing cross cutting aspects, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A customer wants to move its applications from one provider to another cheaply and with little disruption. Which cross-cutting aspect matters most?
notes.back: A: portability.
notes.choices:
A) Portability
B) Interoperability
C) Maintenance and versioning
notes.choicesExplained: B is about interacting with a service and exchanging information predictably, not moving between providers. C is about changes to a service and labelling versions.
notes.explanation: Portability is the ability to move data or applications between providers at low cost and with minimal disruption.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Cloud computing cross cutting aspects, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A customer's systems call a cloud service in the documented way and always get the expected results back. Which cross-cutting aspect does this show?
notes.back: A: interoperability.
notes.choices:
A) Interoperability
B) Portability
C) Auditability
notes.choicesExplained: B is about moving data or applications between providers. C is about making audit evidence available.
notes.explanation: Interoperability is interacting with a cloud service and exchanging information by a prescribed method, with predictable results.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Cloud computing cross cutting aspects, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A customer wants its provider's commitment to 99.95% monthly availability written down, with the service targets identified. What document holds it?
notes.back: A: a service level agreement.
notes.choices:
A) A service level agreement
B) A reversibility plan
C) A governance policy
notes.choicesExplained: B covers retrieving and deleting data at exit. C directs and controls cloud use; it is not the agreement that fixes service targets.
notes.explanation: An SLA is a documented agreement that identifies services and service targets; the cloud SLA sets the quality of the service delivered.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Service levels and service level agreement, PDF p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Is multi-tenancy one of the vocabulary standard's cross-cutting aspects?
notes.back: No. It is one of the six key characteristics; cross-cutting aspects include availability, portability, reversibility and security, among others.
notes.explanation: Cross-cutting aspects are behaviours or capabilities coordinated across roles; multi-tenancy is listed among the key characteristics instead.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Cloud computing cross cutting aspects, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between a cloud capabilities type and a cloud service category?
notes.back: There are only three types, classified by resources used; categories are groups of services with common qualities, each able to span several types.
notes.explanation: Software, Platform and Infrastructure as a Service are categories, each matching one capabilities type; Data Storage as a Service can span all three.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.4, Cloud capabilities types and cloud service categories, PDF p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Special Publication 800-145 has three service models. How many representative cloud service categories does the international vocabulary standard list?
notes.back: Seven: SaaS, PaaS and IaaS plus CaaS, CompaaS, DSaaS and NaaS.
notes.explanation: The standard says it expects further categories to emerge and treats none as more important than another.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.4, Cloud capabilities types and cloud service categories, PDF p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does interoperability differ from portability?
notes.back: Interoperability is exchanging information with a service predictably; portability is moving data or applications between providers.
notes.explanation: The standard says a hybrid cloud's binding technology enables interoperability as well as data and application portability.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Cloud computing cross cutting aspects, PDF p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The international reference architecture has no carrier role. Where does it put the party that provides network connectivity?
notes.back: As the network provider, a sub-role of the cloud service provider.
notes.explanation: The network provider supplies connectivity and network services for customers, partners and the provider, inside or beyond the data centre.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3502 | ISO/IEC 17789:2014, Cloud computing reference architecture, clause 8.3.1.8, CSP:network provider, PDF p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the vocabulary standard, who controls the resources of a public cloud, and who controls those of a private cloud?
notes.back: Public: the cloud service provider. Private: the single cloud service customer using it.
notes.explanation: Control and sharing of resources is exactly how the standard tells deployment models apart.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.5, Cloud deployment models, PDF p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
